clue.text: Small reason for rash, perhaps, to make you smart

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a baby's nappy (diaper) is the cause of nappy rash

explanation.surface: Someone is told a small cause of a skin rash will make them sting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like a verb meaning to sting, tying in with the rash, but it is the adjective meaning well dressed. A NAPPY is the British word for a diaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A snappy dresser is stylish, so snappy is a synonym of smart in the sense of well turned out.

clue.text: Right, perhaps to renounce associate

parts.note: right is one side, an example of a side
to kick a habit is to give it up, renounce it

explanation.surface: Perhaps it is right to give up a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' reads as correct, but it is the right side.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidekick is a close associate or assistant, as Robin is to Batman.

clue.text: One doing tests mid-term after top grades for example

indicators.note: after means the middle letters of term follow the other pieces

parts.note: A is the top grade in exams, so two of them are As
say means for example, as in 'a fruit, say an apple'
the middle letters of the word term are ER

explanation.surface: A student is tested halfway through the term, after top grades for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mid-term' suggests exams, but it means the middle of the word 'term'.
explanation.definitionFit: An assayer tests metals and ores to find their purity or content, so is one doing tests.

clue.text: From top of photo copier, extract bent wire

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter, here of photo

parts.note: an aper is one who apes, a copier or mimic
a clip is an extract from a film

explanation.surface: Someone takes an excerpt from the top of a photocopier using bent wire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Photo copier' suggests an office machine, but it splits into P (top of photo) and APER (one who apes).
explanation.definitionFit: A paperclip is a piece of wire bent into loops to hold sheets of paper together.

clue.text: An American serving time for beginning to peddle subversive material

parts.note: an gives the article A
a GI is an American serviceman
pro means in favour of, so for

indicators.note: the beginning of the word peddle supplies its opening letter only

explanation.surface: An American soldier doing time for starting to deal in seditious literature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serving time' reads as a prison sentence, but 'serving' belongs with 'American' to give GI, and 'time' is T on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitprop is political propaganda, especially left-wing, spread through art and literature to stir up dissent.

clue.text: Three Republicans engaged in my corrupt electoral arrangement

indicators.note: corrupt means spoiled or perverted, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican, so three of them give three Rs

explanation.surface: Three Republicans are involved in my crooked election scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engaged in' looks like a link, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Gerrymandering is redrawing electoral boundaries to favour a party, a corrupt arrangement of voting districts.

clue.text: Shadow cast when just keeping foot on stretcher

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above, so the kept letter sits atop the stretcher
in a down clue the foot of a word is its last letter, so only that letter of cast is kept

parts.note: a rack is an instrument of torture that stretches its victims

explanation.surface: A shadow is cast while someone's foot rests on a stretcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shadow cast' reads as a phrase, but 'Shadow' alone is the definition and 'cast' supplies its last letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: To shadow someone is to follow them closely, which is to track them.

clue.text: Often pouring cups one's filled with dried fruit

indicators.note: to cup something is to hold it inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: a rainy place is one where it often pours
one's is read as 'one is', giving I and IS

explanation.surface: Someone often pours cups of tea filled with dried fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' is read as 'one is', with one as the Roman I; 'cups' looks like teacups but is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Raisiny describes a cake or wine full of raisins, the dried grapes.

clue.text: Little money left: is duty bound not to close till

parts.note: p, a penny, is a small coin in British money

indicators.note: not to close means the last letter is not given, so the word is cut short

parts.note: ought means is under a duty to

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper with little cash left feels obliged to keep the till open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Till' reads as a cash register, but it is the verb to work the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: To till land is to work it for crops, and to plough is to turn it over in the same way.

clue.text: Peer up with chalk, etc, resolved to draw on board

indicators.note: resolved means broken down into parts and reformed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A peer, armed with chalk and so on, is determined to sketch on a blackboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw on board' looks like sketching on a blackboard, but it is a drawn chess game.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, perpetual check is a draw forced by checking the king endlessly, a draw on the board.

clue.text: Like rolls in sauce with fruit to go

indicators.note: the turned word is placed inside the word for sauce

parts.note: a dip is a thick sauce for dunking food

indicators.note: something that rolls turns over, so the word for like is turned round

parts.note: as means like, in 'as good as gold'
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: A diner's bread rolls sit in a dip alongside fruit, as a takeaway order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like bread, but it is the reversal signal. 'To go' suggests takeaway food; 'to' is a link and 'go' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To go, in the sense of vanishing from sight, is to disappear.

clue.text: Every second of long film has repelled friend

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the chosen letters are read backwards
every second letter is taken from the three words long, film and has

explanation.surface: A long film has driven a pal away.
explanation.walkthrough: The second, fourth and following letters of LONG FILM HAS give OGIMA, which turned round gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, used in English as a casual word for a mate or pal.

clue.text: One turned to open bag for filmset supervisor

parts.note: a key is the thing turned in a lock to open it
a grip is a travelling bag, a holdall

explanation.surface: Someone turns a key to open a holdall belonging to a film crew boss.
explanation.walkthrough: On a film set the grips handle camera rigging; the KEY GRIP is the head of that crew.
explanation.definitionFit: The key grip is the chief of the grips, the crew who rig and move camera equipment on a film set.

clue.text: Going on kinky tours with a guide (West End only)

indicators.note: tours suggests going round and about, so the letters travel into a new order
in an across clue the west end of a word is its first letter, so only that letter of guide is kept

explanation.surface: A guide leads kinky tours, but only round London's West End.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's theatre district; here 'West End only' just means the first letter of 'guide'. KINKY, A and G are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Going on means talking at tedious length, which is what yakking describes in informal speech.

clue.text: Jewellery material: gracious lady's left half back

parts.note: Cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like Gracious!

indicators.note: back means the chosen letters are read in reverse
the left half of a word is its first half, so the first two letters of lady

explanation.surface: A jewel maker notes a gracious lady has gone, leaving half behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gracious' looks like a description of the lady, but it stands alone as the British exclamation of surprise; 'left half' and 'back' work on 'lady's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral, the hard skeleton of sea creatures, is polished and worked into beads and other jewellery.

clue.text: Means to take milk and some light refreshments they carry?

parts.note: a teat is what a young animal or baby sucks milk through
rays are beams, some light

explanation.surface: Ways of taking milk and bits of light, with refreshments carried on them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: tea trays are things that carry refreshments, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea trays are what cups, pots and snacks are carried on, so 'refreshments they carry' describes them by their use.

clue.text: Was quick to stock books—-and one did discount

indicators.note: to stock is to hold within, so these letters go inside the word for was quick

parts.note: rushed means went quickly
B is the abbreviation for book, so two of them stand for books
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper hurried to stock books and then sold them off cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discount' looks like a price cut, but means dismiss as worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubbish something is to disparage it as worthless, which is to discount it.

clue.text: Supplies name in the case of Oliver Twist, perhaps

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so the first and last letters of Oliver
in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the twist is a dance popular in the 1960s

explanation.surface: A name appears in the story of Oliver Twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oliver Twist' looks like the Dickens novel, but the two words split: the outside of Oliver, then the twist as an example of a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance is military supplies such as weapons, ammunition and equipment.

clue.text: Pinch collection from dealer in powerful position

parts.note: to whip is British slang for to steal, as is pinch
a hand is the set of cards a card dealer gives each player

explanation.surface: Someone steals the cards a dealer gives out to gain the upper hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinch' looks like a small squeeze, but it means steal. To have the whip hand is to be in control.
explanation.definitionFit: The whip hand is the position of control or advantage over someone, an idiom from the driver holding the whip.

clue.text: Regular shade protects slightly

indicators.note: to protect is to surround and shield, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: a hue is a shade of colour
a bit means slightly, as in 'a bit cold'

explanation.surface: A regular sunshade gives slight protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular' looks like an adjective, but it is the noun for a frequent customer.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitue is a regular visitor to a place, such as a bar or club.

clue.text: One cutting in or abandoning one on world tour

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving out, so the word or is dropped from the longer word

parts.note: an orbiter is a spacecraft circling the world
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cuts in, or gives up on someone travelling round the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link word. 'World tour' suggests a traveller, but it means a satellite or craft in orbit.
explanation.definitionFit: A biter is something that cuts with its teeth, so one cutting into food is a biter.

clue.text: One shot with box camera?

parts.note: a box camera is an old simple camera, but 'box' is also slang for television, so this is a film shot for television

explanation.walkthrough: 'The box' is British slang for television. A box camera was a simple early camera.
explanation.definitionFit: A made-for-television film is one shot for the small screen, the box.

clue.text: Building easy to assemble before cracking

parts.note: pre is a prefix meaning before
fab, short for fabulous, means excellent, as cracking does

explanation.surface: A building that is easy to put together before it starts to crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' suggests breaking, but it is British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: A prefab is a prefabricated building, made in sections for quick assembly on site.

clue.text: So unthinking to deprive of hearing?

parts.note: to rob someone is to deprive them of something
otic is the technical adjective meaning of the ear or of hearing

explanation.surface: Is taking away someone's hearing a mindless act?
explanation.walkthrough: OTIC is the medical word meaning relating to the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting like a machine, without thought, is robotic, so the adjective describes someone so unthinking.

clue.text: Men organised to run in short jacket

parts.note: TU, a trade union, is a body of organised workers

indicators.note: short means the word is cut by its last letter

parts.note: to run in is British slang for to arrest, as is to nick

explanation.surface: Men set up a run wearing short jackets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run in' looks like a race, but it is slang for arrest, NICK, cut short to NIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A tunic is a close-fitting jacket, such as one worn as part of a uniform.

clue.text: One whose job's on the line waving in alarm

definitions.text: One whose job's on the line

indicators.note: waving means moving to and fro, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A worker whose job is at risk waves in alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the line' reads as at risk, but it means working on the railway line.
explanation.definitionFit: A railman is a railway worker, someone whose job is literally on the railway track.

clue.text: Female and I can be compatible

parts.note: taken as written
a tin is a can, as of beans

explanation.surface: A woman says she and her partner can get along.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit in is to be suited to a group or setting, which is to be compatible with it.

clue.text: Rebuilt hospital in East Devon city

indicators.note: rebuilt means put together again differently, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
taken as written
taken as written; Devon is a county in south-west England

explanation.surface: A hospital in East Devon has been reconstructed in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East Devon' looks like the location, but it is fodder: H, IN, E and DEVON are rearranged into a Dutch city.
explanation.definitionFit: Eindhoven is a city in the southern Netherlands, home of the electronics firm Philips.

clue.text: Strong talent European football club found in cup substitute, maybe, missing final

indicators.note: found in means placed inside, so these letters go into the trimmed word
the last letter of the word for a cup substitute is dropped

parts.note: a beaker is a drinking vessel used in place of a cup

explanation.surface: A strong European football club player turns up in a beaker of a cup, short of the final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talent' here is slang for attractive people; 'strong' makes them muscular. 'Cup' and 'final' suggest football trophies, but the cup is a drinking cup.
explanation.definitionFit: Beefcake is slang for muscular, attractive men displayed for admiration; talent is slang for attractive people.

clue.text: Keep present given on promotion

indicators.note: given on means placed after, so the word for present follows the word for promotion

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a promotion
to be here is to be present

explanation.surface: Someone keeps a present that was given to them when they were promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift and 'promotion' like a job move; they are HERE and AD.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere to a rule is to keep to it, so keep in the sense of stick to or observe.
